messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eighteen months ago, during a routine patrol in the arid highlands, Mateo’s convoy struck a buried IED. The blast threw him clear of his Humvee, and in the smoke and ringing silence that followed, he had pulled his squad leader from the wreckage. But when he finally got his bearings, the bodies of his best friend and a fellow mechanic lay scattered behind the shattered cab. Mateo had made a split-second call during the ensuing firefight to prioritize extracting their leader over retrieving their gear—and consequently, their ammunition and med-kits—which cost them two more men. The combat zone was an exposed, sun-baked valley where cover was nonexistent and every ridge line felt like a gun sight waiting to fire. That specific exposure, combined with the weight of survival and tactical failure, anchored the trauma and made the landscape that followed feel perpetually unguarded. At twenty-four, unattached and recently discharged, the memory of that day did not fade; it fractured. When Mateo closed his eyes, the sequence of the blast would slip and rearrange itself—the sound of the detonation would sometimes come before the radio chatter, and the faces of his fallen would blur into a disordered tableau. Because he could not place the events in the correct order, he began to question his own judgment during the firefight. The confusion fed directly into a quiet, grinding conviction that he had acted in ways that go against who he is, violating the core tenets of his training and his own code of brotherhood. He was certain that he had prioritized the wrong objective, and that this moral failure was a permanent stain. That sense of being permanently an outsider to the civilian world he had returned to only deepened the intrusive memories. When Mateo felt disconnected from everyone around him, his mind would automatically search for the trauma to explain his isolation, pulling the vivid details forward like a magnetic pull. Simultaneously, his belief that he had no future led him to construct rigid boundaries to protect himself from further disintegration. He stopped answering calls from old friends, telling himself that talking with others about the event or its aftermath would only drag him back into the pain or force him to confront the grief he was terrified to face. He began to avoid open spaces, viewing exposed areas as psychological mirrors of that sun-baked valley where he had no cover. The sudden return of sensory fragments dictated his daily retreats. When the smell of diesel fuel or the distant report of a backfiring car triggered a flashback of shrapnel tearing through the air, Mateo would immediately step into the nearest alcove, needing physical separation to stop the wave of dread. These avoidance habits compounded over his transition to a career as a financial analyst. His firm’s modern, glass-walled open floor plan became a source of constant physiological arousal. During weekly portfolio reviews, the expansive, unobstructed sightlines would make him feel utterly exposed, as if every colleague were assessing his weakness. To manage the overwhelm, he declined invitations to the firm’s networking lunches and muted his phone to escape any conversation that might veer toward deployments or loss. The consequences were concrete: he missed a critical promotion cycle because he could not engage in the informal mentorship that shaped advancement, and his team noted a sudden, unexplained withdrawal from group strategy sessions. Now, the cycle had grown nearly inescapable. The more Mateo avoided grief reminders and shut down conversations, the more the unresolved memories sharpened, feeding back into his hopelessness. He found himself staring at blank spreadsheets, convinced that no career path or relationship could ever rebuild the shattered certainty he once held about his place in the world. The fragmented flashbacks would return during quiet moments, reminding him of the values he felt he had betrayed, which in turn pushed him to retreat further into isolation. He had come to believe that stepping into an open plaza or speaking about the deployment would only unravel him completely, so he stayed within the confined perimeters of his apartment and his cubicle. What finally brought Mateo to seek help was a panic attack during a client presentation, where the glass walls seemed to close in and the memory of the blast overlaid the projector screen. He sat in the waiting room now, hoping for a way to quiet the repeating fragments, most afraid that he would spend his life permanently detached from everyone, trapped in a past he could never reorder.
